name: Friendmaxxing

card.summary: Deliberately building and upgrading a social circle so that friendships, invitations and introductions lift social standing and dating options alongside physical looks.
card.note: Looksmaxxing-forum guides are anecdotal; research on friendship and wellbeing is correlational.

quick.overview:
Friendmaxxing is the looksmaxxing-culture term for working on your friendships on purpose: meeting more people, choosing a friend group with social standing, and turning online acquaintances into in-person ones. Its appearance payoff, as proponents describe it, is indirect: a friend circle supplies invitations, introductions to women and men, social proof and a steadier mood, which proponents treat as part of how a person comes across.

Beyond forum guides, research on friendship is general rather than specific to the term. Large observational studies link close friendships to better wellbeing and health, though they show association rather than cause. Forum users also discuss it alongside NTmaxxing, the practice of seeming socially 'neurotypical' by grooming, dressing and picking mainstream hobbies.
quick.how: Forum posts describe joining shared-interest groups and games, replying to people who ask for advice, moving from direct messages to voice chat and then to in-person meetups, and choosing friend groups whose members are well-groomed and socially active. Some guides pair it with grooming, clothing and hobby choices so a newcomer fits in at mainstream social settings.
quick.risks: No physical risk is involved. Forum guides disagree about tactics and sometimes discuss avoiding people who drag down status, which critics of such framing say can treat friends as instruments. Meeting internet acquaintances in person carries the usual safety considerations of meeting strangers.

lead: Friendmaxxing is a term from looksmaxxing forums for deliberately building, expanding or upgrading a social circle in order to raise social standing and improve dating and social outcomes.[1][2] It sits in the 'lifestyle' side of the culture rather than the physical-modification side: the idea is that who someone spends time with shapes how they are seen, how often they are invited out, and whom they meet.[2]

On looksmax.org, users describe tactics such as befriending forum members through shared games, moving to social-media contact and then in-person meetups, and choosing friend groups with higher status.[1][2] A related thread format, 'NTmaxxing', gives advice on appearing socially mainstream, covering grooming, clean clothes, conventional hobbies and basic social skills, and in one guide treats good looks as a precondition for being included.[3]

No studies test friendmaxxing as a practice. General research on friendship, summarized on Wikipedia, associates close friendships with better wellbeing, self-esteem and health, though most of that work is correlational.[4]

chain: Meet more people and choose a higher-status circle
More invitations, introductions and social proof
Better social and dating opportunities and mood
angle.text: Friendmaxxers treat a friend group as part of a person's overall presentation: friends provide invitations, introductions and a confident social baseline that make looks and personality easier to display. It is practiced by joining communities, converting online contacts into in-person ones and pairing it with grooming and style.

paras: The term applies the '-maxxing' suffix of looksmaxxing culture to friendships: optimizing the number, quality and standing of one's social ties. Forum authors frame friend groups as affecting social life, mental wellbeing and dating life, and illustrate this with accounts of their own past friend groups.[2]

Some posters extend the idea to shared living: one thread describes converting online friends into in-person friends and eventually pooling rent in a shared house, a plan other users answered with skepticism.[1]

A long-running looksmax.org thread on NTmaxxing and friendmaxxing lists what the author considers prerequisites: decent looks (the author cites a minimum of about 4 on the PSL scale), clean clothes, good grooming and skin, conventional hobbies and no speech problems, and recommends finding a niche group that matches one's interests.[3] Replies range from agreement that the guide is useful to remarks that needing one means a person is already struggling socially.[3]
A separate guide by a user describes the author's successive friend groups from childhood onward and how each affected mood and social life.[2]

Research on friendship generally links close friendships with greater happiness, self-esteem and better health in adults and with protection against anxiety and depression in adolescents; reviews note that most of these are correlations and causation is not established.[4] A 2023 eLife study reported that benefits for mental health and cognition rose with number of close friends up to around five and not beyond.[4]

lore.intro: Friendmaxxing threads on looksmax.org mix tactical advice, personal anecdote and banter about how much social skills matter relative to looks.[1][2][3]

claims.claim: Befriending people online can be converted into real-life friendships.
claims.believers: One user says he has befriended several forum members by answering advice requests, finding shared games and moving to social apps, then meeting in person.[1]
claims.experts: No published research has examined this forum strategy specifically.

claims.claim: Your friend group strongly shapes your dating life and mental wellbeing.
claims.believers: A guide author argues friend groups affect social life, mood and dating and illustrates it with his own history.[2]
claims.experts: General friendship research associates close friendships with better wellbeing, though studies are largely correlational.[4]

claims.claim: Looks and grooming come first, then social integration ('NTmaxxing').
claims.believers: One guide says people should looksmax before NTmaxxing and keep hobbies conventional so as not to be excluded.[3]
claims.experts: No published studies test this ordering.
